boardQuestions.answer: 1) Dynastic succession means the control of a party passing to the family members of its leaders, irrespective of their ability, as when sons, daughters or relatives occupy the top posts. 2) It is a challenge because ordinary and capable workers lose the chance to rise, decisions concentrate in one family and the party's image of public service weakens. 3) Voters then begin to see politics as family property, which lowers the quality of democracy.

boardQuestions.question: What are the conditions laid down for a party to be recognised as a national party or a state party in India?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) National party: a party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four states and, in addition, wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha is recognised as a national party and gets a common symbol across the country. 2) State party: a party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in an Assembly election of a state and wins at least two seats is recognised as a state party, also called a regional party. 3) Recognition is granted by the Election Commission, which also allots symbols; examples of national parties are the BJP, Congress, BSP, CPI, CPI(M) and NPP, while parties like the Biju Janata Dal are state parties.

boardQuestions.question: Explain any three major challenges faced by political parties in India.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Lack of internal democracy: many parties do not keep membership registers, do not hold organisational meetings regularly and do not conduct internal elections, so power concentrates in a few top leaders. 2) Dynastic succession: leaders promote relatives to top positions, blocking capable and ordinary workers and reducing the party to family property. 3) Money and muscle power: parties prefer rich candidates or those with muscle backing, and in some cases candidates facing criminal cases are chosen because they can fund campaigns and win, which short-circuits the democratic process. 4) In addition, the ideological differences among parties have narrowed, so voters often do not get a meaningful choice of programmes.

boardQuestions.question: Why are political parties essential in a democracy? Describe any five functions of political parties.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Contest elections: parties select and field candidates who seek the people's mandate; without parties no representative government can be organised. 2) Offer policies: parties put forward different policies and programmes, and voters choose among these options, which converts public demands into political agendas. 3) Make laws: parties play a decisive role in law making, since members vote along party lines and the majority party carries its programme through the legislature. 4) Form and run governments: parties recruit leaders, train them and run the administration at the Union, state and local levels. 5) Play the opposition: defeated parties criticise the government, voice different views and keep a check on the misuse of power. 6) Shape public opinion: parties raise and highlight issues, launch movements and use media and speeches to shape what citizens think. 7) Provide access: local leaders of parties act as a link between citizens and government machinery, helping people use welfare schemes and get grievances heard. 8) Conclusion: because parties aggregate interests, offer choices and make accountability possible, they are indispensable instruments of democracy despite their flaws. 9) Most of all, parties connect citizens to the system between elections, which no other institution can do at the same scale, so the health of parties decides the health of democracy itself.

boardQuestions.question: Political parties need reform. Describe the steps already taken to reform them and suggest further measures that could strengthen parties in India.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Anti-defection law: the Constitution was amended in 1985 so that an elected representative who leaves the party on whose symbol he or she was elected loses the seat; this checked the horse-trading of legislators. 2) Affidavit rule: on the direction of the Supreme Court, every candidate must file an affidavit disclosing property and criminal cases pending against him or her, which lets voters judge candidates. 3) Election Commission orders: the ECI made it compulsory for parties to hold their organisational elections and to file their income tax returns, increasing internal transparency. 4) Suggested reforms: a law should regulate the internal affairs of parties, making it compulsory to maintain registers of members, to follow their own constitutions, to hold regular internal elections and to have an independent authority to judge party disputes. 5) The state should consider funding elections partly from public money so that parties are not captured by big donors, along with guarantees of media access. 6) Quotas for women candidates would improve representation inside parties and in legislatures and bring new talent into politics and decision making. 7) Conclusion: reforms must touch both money and internal democracy, because parties are the gatekeepers of democracy and only healthy parties can deliver healthy governments.

boardQuestions.question: Read the following source and answer the sub-questions: 'A veteran leader's son-in-law and nephew hold the top posts of a party that has not held internal elections for a decade. Candidates are chosen mainly for their ability to spend on the campaign, and one nominee faces several criminal cases. Ordinary members complain that they learn of important decisions only from television.' (a) Which challenges of political parties does the passage reflect? (b) Explain any two reforms that could address these problems. (c) What role does the Election Commission play in reforming parties?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) The passage reflects dynastic succession, since family members of the leader hold the top posts, and the growing role of money and muscle power, since candidates are chosen for spending capacity and one nominee faces criminal cases. 2) It also shows lack of internal democracy, as there have been no internal elections and ordinary members are ignored. 3) (b) An effective internal democracy law should force parties to maintain membership registers, hold organisational elections at fixed intervals and settle disputes before an independent authority. 4) Mandatory disclosure through affidavits of assets and criminal cases, already in force, should be strictly enforced so that voters can reject tainted candidates. 5) State funding of elections and free media access would reduce dependence on big donors. 6) (c) The Election Commission registers parties, grants recognition, allots symbols and compels parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns. 7) It monitors campaign conduct, checks malpractices and can act against parties that violate rules, making it the most important institutional force for party reform. 8) Together, internal reforms and external monitoring can restore people's trust in parties. 9) When these measures work together, dynastic control and money power lose their grip and parties again serve the public interest that justifies their existence.

chapters.title: Outcomes of Democracy
chapters.summary: Democracy must be judged by its outcomes: an accountable, responsive and legitimate government, economic growth with less inequality, accommodation of social diversity, and dignity with freedom. Its growth record is mixed, but no alternative regime matches its legitimacy, dignity and freedom. This chapter trains you to evaluate democracy as both a promise and a performance.
hotTopics: Dignity of women and oppressed castes

sections.heading: How to Judge Democracy - the Five Expected Outcomes
points: Democracy should be judged on its outcomes, not only on its promises; the chapter checks five broad expectations.
Expectation one: democracy should produce an accountable, responsive and legitimate government.
Expectations two and three: democracy should promote economic growth and development, and it should reduce inequality and poverty.
Expectation four: democracy should accommodate social diversity; expectation five: it should ensure the dignity and freedom of citizens.
No government is perfectly democratic, but these five tests let citizens evaluate how far democracy is actually delivering.

keyTerms.meaning: The actual result of a political system's working, judged against what it promises.
The things citizens rightly expect from democracy, such as accountability, equality, accommodation and freedom.

sections.trick: Remember A-L-G-I-A-D-F in pairs: Accountable-Legitimate, Growth-Inequality, Accommodate diversity, Dignity-Freedom - the five outcomes in four pairs.
sections.examPointer: The five outcomes are the chapter's answer skeleton; open any 5-marker by listing them, then expand on the ones the question asks.

sections.heading: Accountable, Responsive and Legitimate Government
points: A democratic government is legitimate because it is elected by citizens and rests on their consent; people wish to be ruled by representatives they choose themselves.
Democracy creates mechanisms through which citizens can hold the government accountable and make it work according to set procedures.
Democratic governments are expected to be responsive to the needs and expectations of the people; if they fail, citizens can question, correct and change them.
Democratic decision making involves consultation and debate, which makes governments slower than non-democratic rulers, who need to consult no one.
But consultation prevents rash decisions, and the ability of citizens to remove governments matters more than speed, so democracy's legitimacy outweighs its slowness.

keyTerms.meaning: The acceptance of a government's right to rule because citizens chose it themselves.
The obligation of a government to answer to citizens for its actions and decisions.
The willingness of a government to act on people's needs and grievances.

sections.trick: ARL badge: Accountable, Responsive, Legitimate - picture 'A Responsible Leader' wearing it.
sections.examPointer: 'Why is democracy called a legitimate government?' is a high-frequency 3-marker; add the efficiency-versus-consultation contrast for full marks in 5-markers.

sections.heading: Economic Growth and Development
points: When the growth records of all democracies and all dictatorships are compared for 1950 to 2000, dictatorships show only a slightly higher rate of economic growth, a difference too small to prove superiority.
Growth depends on the economic conditions of a country and the priorities of its rulers more than on the form of government, so regime type alone does not decide development.
For poorer countries too, the gap in growth between the two kinds of regimes is small, which breaks the myth that only dictatorships can deliver rapid development.
Within democracies, development outcomes vary according to the goals chosen by those in power; priorities such as education, health and welfare shape living standards.
Hence democracy's economic report card is mixed: it is not a guarantee of prosperity, but neither is it an obstacle to growth.

keyTerms.meaning: The increase in the output of goods and services of a country over time.
The broader improvement in living standards, education, health and opportunities, beyond mere growth.

sections.trick: Use the line 'Growth is about priorities and conditions, not about regime type' to answer any growth comparison question.
sections.examPointer: MCQs test the conclusion that there is no decisive difference in growth, not decimal figures; 3-markers ask why growth varies - answer with conditions and priorities.

sections.heading: Reduction of Inequality and Poverty
points: Democracies are based on political equality, in which every adult citizen has one vote of equal value.
Yet economic inequalities persist and often grow in democracies, and in actual life democracies have not been very successful in reducing them.
A small section of ultra-rich people commands a hugely disproportionate share of wealth and incomes, while the bottom 20 per cent of the population shares a very small slice of national income.
Poverty and deprivation remain realities in many democracies, though democratic politics gives the poor channels such as elections, courts and movements to demand action.
The coexistence of political equality and economic inequality shows that reducing inequality is an unfinished democratic struggle, not an automatic result.

keyTerms.meaning: The equal right of every adult citizen to vote and contest elections.
The unequal distribution of income and wealth among the members of a society.

sections.trick: 'One vote, many incomes' - memorise this phrase; it captures the paradox examiners want you to explain.
sections.examPointer: A common 2 or 3-marker asks you to justify that democracy has not reduced inequality; pair political equality against economic disparity in your answer.

sections.heading: Accommodation of Social Diversity
points: No society can fully and permanently resolve conflicts among different groups, but democracy can learn to respect differences and evolve procedures to negotiate them.
Democracy is best suited for this outcome because it gives every social group channels to express grievances and to seek redressal.
Majority rule in democracy means that the option preferred by more voters is chosen; it never means permanent rule of one community over others.
To keep majority rule just, the majority always needs to work with the minority, so that the government functions on the basis of consent rather than domination.
Belgium's accommodation of its Dutch and French speakers contrasts with Sri Lanka's majoritarianism, showing that respect for diversity reduces the possibility of conflict.

keyTerms.meaning: Negotiating social differences by giving every group a place and voice in decision making.
In democracy, the option or candidate preferred by more than half of the voters - not a single community ruling permanently.

sections.trick: 'Majority means more voters, not one community' - write this line whenever a question uses the phrase rule by majority.
sections.examPointer: Cross-chapter 5-markers link this section with Belgium and Sri Lanka; use one country as the positive case and the other as the warning.

sections.heading: Dignity and Freedom of Citizens
points: Democracy stands much superior to any other form of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual, because it recognises the intrinsic equality of all human beings.
Every individual, whatever his or her wealth, caste or gender, deserves equal respect; this claim becomes an enforceable right only under democratic politics.

Dignity of women: democratic politics has given feminist movements a platform, and their struggles have won the vote, education rights, reservation in local bodies and now a law for reservation in legislatures.

Dignity of oppressed castes: the constitutional abolition of untouchability, equality before law and political assertion by Dalits and other deprived groups have challenged the caste hierarchy and expanded self-respect.

Freedom: democracy allows citizens to express dissent, practise their faith, choose their occupations and claim rights, and every exercise of freedom raises expectations that governments must then honour.
The expansion of democracy means that people can raise demands, debate them publicly and get them addressed over time - an ability that no dictatorship offers.

keyTerms.meaning: The idea that every human being has equal worth irrespective of wealth, caste or gender.
The open expression of disagreement with those in power, which democracy protects.
The continuous widening of democracy's scope - more rights, more inclusion and deeper participation.

sections.trick: DEF kit: Dignity (of women and castes), Equality (intrinsic worth), Freedom (dissent and choice) - democracy's permanent gifts.
sections.examPointer: 'Democracy promotes dignity and freedom' is a very high probability 5-marker; always use women and oppressed castes as your two examples and close with the expansion line.

mcqs.question: A democratic government is called legitimate because:
options: it is elected by the people and rules with their consent
mcqs.explanation: Legitimacy rests on consent: a democratic government is elected by the people, so its decisions are accepted as right. Efficiency is not the basis of legitimacy.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an expected outcome of democracy?
mcqs.explanation: Reduction of inequality and poverty is one of the five expected outcomes of democracy. The other options belong to authoritarian systems.

mcqs.question: In a democracy, the people can change a government they dislike through:
mcqs.explanation: Regular elections let citizens remove a government that fails them. This is the core mechanism that makes democracy accountable.

mcqs.question: Democracy promotes which of the following?
options: Dignity and freedom of the individual
mcqs.explanation: Democracy is superior to other forms of government in promoting dignity and freedom, because it recognises the intrinsic equality of all human beings.

mcqs.question: Non-democratic regimes sometimes appear more efficient because:
options: they do not have to consult anyone before taking decisions
mcqs.explanation: Non-democratic rulers can act quickly because they need not consult anyone or answer to anyone. Their speed, however, can produce rash decisions.

mcqs.question: Comparing all democracies and dictatorships between 1950 and 2000, the conclusion on economic growth is that:
options: dictatorships show only a slightly higher growth, so there is no decisive difference
growth is identical in both systems
mcqs.explanation: Over 1950 to 2000 dictatorships recorded only a slightly higher rate of growth than democracies. The difference is too small to prove that one regime type is superior.

mcqs.question: In actual life, democracies have been:
options: fully successful in abolishing economic inequality
not very successful in reducing economic inequalities
forbidden by law from having inequality
identical to dictatorships in every respect
mcqs.explanation: Despite political equality, economic inequalities persist and often grow in democracies. Reducing inequality remains an unfinished democratic struggle.

mcqs.question: Majority rule in a democracy means:
options: permanent rule of the majority community
choosing the option preferred by more voters while working with minorities
mcqs.explanation: Majority rule means the choice of the option or candidate preferred by more voters. It never justifies permanent domination by one community, so the majority must work with the minority.

mcqs.question: Why is accommodation of social diversity important in a democracy?
options: It allows the majority community to dominate permanently
It reduces the possibility of conflict by respecting and negotiating differences
It ends all social differences forever
mcqs.explanation: Democracy accommodates diversity by giving every group channels to express grievances, which reduces conflict. No society can erase differences, but they can be negotiated.

mcqs.question: Which statement best captures the chapter's argument on dignity and freedom?
options: Democracy creates a platform on which disadvantaged groups can claim dignity and expand freedom over time
Freedom exists only on election day
mcqs.explanation: Democracy recognises the intrinsic equality of every person and lets disadvantaged groups, such as women and oppressed castes, raise demands and expand their freedom over time. Change is gradual, not instant.

boardQuestions.question: Why is a democratic government considered a legitimate government?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) A democratic government is legitimate because it is elected by the people and rules with their consent; citizens wish to be governed by representatives chosen by themselves. 2) Laws and policies made by such a government are accepted as right even when people dislike a particular decision. 3) Non-democratic rulers may be efficient, but without consent their power lacks acceptance and can survive only by force.

boardQuestions.question: 'Democracy has not been very successful in reducing economic inequalities.' Justify this statement.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Democracies rest on political equality, as every adult has one vote of equal value, yet economic inequalities persist and often grow. 2) A small group of ultra-rich people enjoys a highly disproportionate share of wealth and incomes, while the bottom 20 per cent of the population shares very little of the national income. 3) Hence, in actual life, democracies have not been very successful in reducing economic inequalities, proving that political equality alone cannot guarantee economic equality.

boardQuestions.question: Democratic governments are often slow and less efficient. Why? Why is this not really a defect of democracy?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Democratic governments look slow because decisions involve consultation, debate among representatives, respect for procedures and consideration of different groups' interests. 2) Non-democratic rulers can act quickly since they do not have to consult or answer to anyone, so they may appear more efficient. 3) But speed without consent can produce rash and one-sided decisions, while consultation reduces the chances of irresponsible decisions. 4) Moreover, a democratic government can be questioned, corrected and changed by citizens, so its mistakes do not become permanent. 5) Hence deliberation is not a defect; it is the price of a government that is accountable, responsive and legitimate.

boardQuestions.question: How does democracy accommodate social diversity? Explain with examples.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) No society can permanently resolve conflicts among its groups, but democracy learns to respect differences and to negotiate them through accepted procedures. 2) Majority rule in democracy means the option preferred by more voters wins; it never means permanent rule by one community, so the majority must always work with the minority and share power with it. 3) Democracy gives every social group, whether religious, linguistic or caste-based, channels to express grievances and demand redressal, as reserved constituencies, women's reservation and community governments show. 4) By accommodating diversity, democracies reduce the possibility of violent conflict, as Belgium's accommodation contrasts with Sri Lanka's majoritarianism.

boardQuestions.question: 'Democracy promotes the dignity and freedom of citizens.' Explain this statement with examples.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Democracy stands superior to every other form of government in promoting dignity and freedom of the individual, because it recognises the intrinsic equality of all human beings. 2) Dignity of women: in patriarchal societies women's work and worth are undervalued, but democratic politics has given feminist movements a platform, and their struggles have secured the vote, education rights, reservation in local bodies and now a law for reservation in legislatures. 3) Dignity of oppressed castes: the constitutional abolition of untouchability, equality before law and political assertion by Dalits and other deprived groups have challenged the caste hierarchy and given them voice and self-respect. 4) Freedom: democracy provides an environment in which citizens can express dissent, practise any faith, choose their occupations and claim their rights without fear; every expansion of freedom raises expectations that governments must honour. 5) People can raise demands, debate them publicly and get them addressed over time, which no dictatorship allows. 6) Conclusion: by turning dignity and freedom from privileges into claims, democracy transforms citizens from subjects into participants. 7) It is this constant expansion - new rights claimed and new voices heard - that keeps democracy alive and makes it superior to every closed and unequal system.

boardQuestions.question: Evaluate the economic outcomes of democracy with reference to growth, development and inequality.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Growth: comparing all democracies and all dictatorships over 1950 to 2000, dictatorships show only a slightly higher rate of economic growth, a difference too small to prove superiority; growth depends on economic conditions and the priorities of governments rather than on the regime type. 2) Poorer countries: among poorer nations too the gap between the two kinds of regimes is small, so democracy is not an obstacle to development. 3) Inequality: democracies are based on political equality but have not been very successful in reducing economic inequalities; the richest sections command a hugely disproportionate share of income and wealth while the bottom 20 per cent shares very little. 4) Poverty and deprivation persist in many democracies, though citizens can pressure governments through elections, courts and movements. 5) Development: within democracies, outcomes vary with the goals those in power choose; when governments prioritise education, health and welfare, living standards improve. 6) Conclusion: democracy's economic report card is mixed but not worse than the alternatives, and its open politics gives citizens the tools to demand better performance, which closed regimes deny. 7) In the long run, the freedom to criticise, vote and organise is itself an economic asset, because it exposes failure early and forces correction that closed regimes postpone.

boardQuestions.question: Read the following source and answer the sub-questions: 'In country A, an elected government lost power after its failure to control prices, and the courts ordered an inquiry into a minister's conduct. In country B, a military ruler built highways rapidly and jailed his critics; no election has been held for thirty years, and newspapers cannot question his decisions.' (a) Which government is accountable to its people? Give reasons. (b) Does rapid development justify rule without consent? Explain. (c) State any two merits of democracy shown by this comparison.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) Country A's government is accountable because citizens could vote it out for failing on prices, and independent courts could question even ministers; authority in country A flows from the people and can be withdrawn through regular, free elections. 2) (b) Rapid construction is only one measure of performance; a regime that jails critics and silences newspapers can build highways but cannot secure dignity, freedom or honest feedback. 3) Without consent, mistakes remain hidden because no one dares to point them out, and policies reflect the ruler's will rather than the people's needs, so failures accumulate silently. 4) Speed gained by silencing citizens is therefore not true effectiveness; development that ignores freedom remains incomplete, unjust and often unsustainable. 5) (c) Merit one: democracy produces an accountable and legitimate government, so wrong decisions can be questioned, corrected and changed by the people themselves. 6) Merit two: democracy protects dignity and freedom, allowing citizens and the media to criticise rulers without fear, which keeps governance honest. 7) Consultation and debate also reduce the chance of rash decisions, even though they take time. 8) Hence country A's slower but answerable politics serves its citizens better than country B's fast but unanswerable rule.
